svg.aria-label: Diagram: Azure custom roles, showing that AssignableScopes does two jobs at once by deciding both where a custom role may be assigned and who may create, update or delete it, the six hard limits including no root scope, no wildcards in AssignableScopes, one management group only and 5,000 custom roles per tenant, the DataActions rule that such a role cannot be assigned at management group scope but can be assigned at subscriptions within one, and the deletion path that requires removing every role assignment including PIM-eligible ones first
svg.title: Azure custom roles: AssignableScopes decides both where the role can be used and who owns it, and every limit on it is fixed
svg.text: AssignableScopes is not a deployment target. It is the role’s ownership boundary.
One property decides where the role can be assigned and, separately, who is allowed to create, update or delete it.
Job 1 — where the role may be assigned
Management groups, subscriptions and resource groups.
A subscription listed here also covers every resource group
and resource inside it.
Access is decided by the assignment, not by this list.
Define broadly, assign narrowly.
Job 2 — who may manage the role itself
Creating, updating or deleting a custom role requires
Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/write
on every scope in AssignableScopes — not any one of them.
Add a subscription you do not administer and you can no
longer edit your own role.
The limits, all fixed — none of these can be raised by asking
Custom roles per tenant
5,000 — a directory-wide budget, shared by every subscription in the tenant
AssignableScopes per role
Management groups in that list
exactly 1, and Resource Manager does not validate that it exists
Root scope
not allowed — built-in roles use it, custom roles never can
Wildcards in AssignableScopes
not allowed, so nobody can reach a new scope by editing the role definition
Wildcards in an action string
one only — and it silently adopts every future action that matches
Role name
must be unique across the whole tenant; the role ID survives a rename
DataActions and management groups
A custom role with DataActions cannot be assigned at
management group scope.
But it may still name one there.
Define once with the management group in AssignableScopes,
then assign it at the subscriptions inside it — one role instead
of one per subscription.
Deleting one is the expensive direction
RoleDefinitionHasAssignments
Every assignment using the role must be removed first —
found by iterating the role’s own AssignableScopes, which is
the second thing that list is for.
Including PIM-eligible assignments, which no Resource
Graph query over active assignments will show you.
The case for writing one: a custom role spends fewer role assignments
A subscription allows 4,000 role assignments and the limit is fixed. Where one principal holds three built-in roles at one scope, a single
custom role carrying the same actions replaces all three — two assignments returned to the budget, per principal, per scope.
This is Microsoft’s own documented remedy for the limit, alongside group-based assignments and making assignments eligible.
The case against: a wildcard in a custom role reproduces exactly the defect that makes Contributor the wrong default — it adopts
actions that do not exist yet. The difference is that now the role is yours, and nobody at Microsoft reviews what it grew into.
Sources: Azure custom roles, role definitions, troubleshoot Azure RBAC limits, and Azure subscription and service limits, on Microsoft Learn.
